card.title: I Spent $7,000,000 On My Animated Series
card.sub_style: likely: anime-influenced 2D TV-series animation shown in a high-budget behind-the-scenes and trailer format, comparing the old and new art styles
card.summary: This is a 4-minute-20-second promo for the new season of the Beast Animations series, released two days before Episode 1 (November 1). Judging by the title, description and comments, it uses the $7M budget as a hook, shows the artists and writers behind the show, and includes clips that viewers compare to anime and Ben 10. It's worth studying as a way to market an animated series by revealing the process and production scale. As a craft reference it's weak: the most-liked craft comment calls the animation 'stiff' and lacking fluidity.
how_it_is_made: likely: Open on a big-number hook (the $7,000,000 budget in the title) to frame the series as a spectacle before showing any animation.
likely: Cut between interviews or footage of the team and finished animation clips. The description says 'So many people worked so hard', and commenters praise 'hiring real artists and writers'.
likely: Around 0:34, address what to call the show. Commenters note he 'refuses to call it an anime', so the video seems to deliberately use the word 'animation'.
likely: Around 0:47, refer to Eiichiro Oda ('The legend Oda-sensei'). This could be a reference, a cameo or an endorsement; the source doesn't say which.
likely: Around 1:23, compare the previous season's art style with the new one in a self-deprecating way ('Bro dissing his own style').
likely: Around 3:56, show an action or transformation clip in a Western-cartoon style ('giving me Ben 10 vibes').
likely: Close by pointing to the Episode 1 premiere date and the other channels to drive viewers onward. A pinned creator comment links to Episode 1 once it's live.

likely: Production pipeline: a studio-scale 2D pipeline with script, storyboard/animatic, key and in-between animation, compositing, and voice acting (a VA commenter suggests voice acting is involved). The comments suggest it's animated on low-frame-rate holds (on 2s/3s or limited animation).

evidence.claim: The hook is the budget figure, not the animation itself.
evidence.quote: I Spent $7,000,000 On My Animated Series

evidence.claim: The video is a behind-the-scenes look at the team that made the season.
evidence.quote: So many people worked so hard on the new season of Beast Animations, and I can't wait for you guys to see it :)

evidence.claim: Showing human artists, set against AI-generated content, is a strong emotional driver for the audience.
evidence.quote: love how theres invested in real artists and not just AI slop (408 likes)

evidence.claim: Viewers find the motion stiff and low in frame rate, which counts against timing and fluidity.
evidence.quote: it still feels rather stiff and lacks fluidity. You need to increase the frame rate (frames per second) (3,300 likes)

evidence.claim: Viewers place the work against familiar references (anime, Ben 10, Oda), mixing novelty with familiarity, and there is debate over whether it counts as anime.
evidence.quote: I love how he refuses to call it an anime 😂 / 3:56 This giving me Ben 10 vibes

evidence.claim: Production depends on a large studio budget, so a solo creator can't easily reproduce it.
evidence.quote: I swear if you invested that much money in japanese or chinese animation studio the result would be 1000 time better..

evidence.claim: Comparing the old style with the new one is part of the process reveal.
evidence.quote: 1:23 Bro dissing his own style😂

open_questions: Which animation software and studio(s) made the series? Neither is named in the source.
What frame rate or animation cadence does it use (on 2s, 3s, limited)? The comments call it stiff, but there are no frames to check.
What happens at 0:47? Is Eiichiro Oda appearing, endorsing it, or only being referenced?
How much of the 260s runtime is finished animation versus BTS/interview footage?
The creator follower count of 10 doesn't fit 20.6M views. It's probably a data error or a stale figure for a new channel, so views-per-follower is unreliable.
How sound design and music are timed to the animation is unknown, because there's no audio or transcript.
The top comment is political and unrelated to the craft. Does it reflect brigading that inflates the comment count?

card.title: Dangerous Blind Spot (3D) by Professor of How
card.sub_style: Stylised 3D road-safety explainer short with a caricature character (a truck/bus driver that viewers read as a public-figure lookalike)
card.summary: An 82-second 3D short from Professor Of How. The title suggests it explains a dangerous blind spot around a large vehicle. It got 15.5M views in about 12 days, roughly 0.96 views per follower. The comments are not about the safety lesson. They are about the truck/bus driver character, who viewers say looks like Narendra Modi, and about another character's hairstyle. The useful takeaway is that a recognisable caricature can drive engagement on an educational 3D short. That lesson rests on the comments, not on any frames, so treat it carefully.
how_it_is_made: likely: Script one hazard ('blind spot' around a truck/bus) as a short cause-and-effect story under ~90 s, with a setup, the dangerous moment, and the lesson.

likely: Model or kitbash a large vehicle (truck/bus), a road environment, and a small number of stylised characters. Viewers repeatedly call it a truck and also a bus, so the vehicle type is uncertain.
likely: Design the driver as a stylised character with recognisable features. Viewers widely say he 'looks like Modi ji'. The source does not say whether the likeness was intended.
likely: Give a second character a distinctive hairstyle as a visual hook. Comments single out 'Bhai ki hair style' and 'new haircut'.
likely: Visualise the blind spot from the driver's viewpoint and/or as an overhead zone so the viewer can see what the driver cannot.
likely: Animate the near-miss or collision, then end on a takeaway. One comment suggests the video raises the idea of camera systems ('A 360-degree camera system should be mandatory for the trucks').
likely: Render in vertical or short-form format and publish to YouTube under the channel's '(3D)' title convention.

card.title: Building Real-Time Animation with Gemini 4 Argon
card.sub_style: Agent-generated real-time code animation with procedural/generative audio and custom tools built by the agent, using no external media assets (product demo)
card.summary: A 136-second product demo from Google Antigravity showing the Gemini 4 Argon model inside its agent IDE producing real-time animation, generative audio and custom tooling entirely from code, with no imported images, footage or sound files. It matters to motion designers as a sign of where code-only, agent-driven generative motion is going. It is not a craft reference for timing or easing, because the source says nothing about the animation itself. Viewer interest centres on the model and who can access it, not on the animation craft.
how_it_is_made: Open a project in Google Antigravity with Gemini 4 Argon selected as the agent model (the creator states both the platform and the model).
Prompt the agent to build the animation as code only, with no external media assets: every visual and every sound has to come from code.
likely: the agent writes a real-time renderer (e.g. a browser canvas/WebGL or shader loop) that draws the visuals procedurally every frame instead of playing back pre-rendered frames.

likely: the agent writes generative audio code (e.g. Web Audio-style oscillators and envelopes) instead of loading sample files, since the description says 'generative audio' and 'without external media assets'.
likely: the agent builds custom tools (e.g. parameter panels or sliders) so a human can direct the motion live. The description says 'custom tool-building'.
likely: subagents explore several visual directions in parallel and the human picks one. This comes from a single viewer comment, not from the creator.
likely: preview in the browser the agent controls, adjust through more prompts, then screen-record the result for the demo.

evidence.claim: The novelty is that everything (visuals, audio and tools) comes from code, with no imported assets.

likely: Give the cooking sequence its own step-by-step shots, because the food scenes keep viewers watching and draw comments about traditional food.

card.title: Prada Holiday 2026 | "Drawing Prada: Animated by Hand"
card.sub_style: live-action celebrity footage composited with hand-drawn 2D character animation (whimsical winter animals and scenes), luxury holiday ad
card.summary: A 54-second Prada holiday campaign film that places live-action talent inside hand-drawn animated winter scenes. The cast is Prada Ambassadors Chen Haoyu, Sadie Sink, Maya Hawke and Kelvin Harrison Jr., "together with Luther Ford". It reached about 3M views (7.17 views per follower). The comments focus on the hand-drawn, AI-free framing and praise the human craft more than the fashion. The celebrity cast probably also helped the reach. It is a useful case study in how visibly hand-made production can become both a talking point and a sign of luxury.
how_it_is_made: likely: Write the concept and storyboard winter vignettes so the cast's live-action blocking leaves space for animated characters and environments to be added later.
likely: Shoot the cast in live action (likely against plain or partly built sets), recording eyelines and contact points where animated characters will interact.

likely: Pull reference frames from the plates and do rough 2D character animation on top of them, frame by frame (a viewer comment credits former Disney/Don Bluth animator John Pomeroy with the animals; the creator does not confirm this).
likely: Clean up line work, then add colour and tone to the drawings in an illustrated, storybook winter palette.
likely: Paint or illustrate the backgrounds and environment layers so the scenes read as 'environments of pure imagination'.
likely: Composite the animation over the live-action plates, matching contact shadows, light wrap and grain so the two layers feel like one world.
likely: Edit to 54s with a holiday score and add the closing branding.

card.title: My Chemical Romance & Lauren Tsai - Prelude to The End (An Animated Short Film)

card.title: How LAIKA Studios Made Their Most Advanced Stop-Motion Puppet
card.sub_style: Behind-the-scenes armature breakdown of a feature-film stop-motion puppet: a golden eagle with a complex engineered armature, shown by the armaturist in a long-form interview
card.summary: In this 22-minute Tested video, Adam Savage interviews LAIKA senior armaturist Jeanne McIvor about The General, a golden eagle puppet from Wildwood. The description calls it "the most advanced stop-motion puppet they've ever created", with an armature that lets animators control "every muscle and feather". The video is not a finished animation. It shows the engineering that makes frame-by-frame performance possible, so it is most useful to designers studying puppet rigging and how behind-the-scenes content gets made. Only the title, description, tags, metrics and comments were available. No frames, audio or transcript.
how_it_is_made: likely: Design the character with real anatomy as the reference. A biologist commenter says the armature 'can almost be used to teach bird skeletal anatomy'.
Spend years developing the armature. The description says it 'took years of development to create'.
likely: Machine metal joints, such as ball-and-socket and hinge joints, that hold a pose under the weight of the puppet's covering from frame to frame.
Build a spiral-shaped neck skeleton. A commenter calls it 'The spiral neck skeleton'. likely: this lets the neck bend smoothly in many directions instead of in stiff jointed steps.

Add controls for individual muscles and feathers; the description says the features 'allowed animators to control every muscle and feather'. likely: animators use these to adjust the eagle's silhouette and shift its feathers a little in each frame.
likely: Put skin and feather coverings over the armature, then animate frame by frame on set, nudging the joints between exposures.
For the BTS video: record a host-and-expert walkthrough of the bare armature and its features, then publish it while the film is in theaters so it doubles as promotion.

evidence.claim: The title and description hook with a superlative claim about the puppet.
evidence.quote: the most advanced stop-motion puppet they've ever created

evidence.claim: The whole video is a process reveal: the armaturist explains how the puppet was built and what it can do.
evidence.quote: Senior armaturist Jeanne McIvor walks Adam through its fabrication and the features that allowed animators to control every muscle and feather on this majestic bird.

evidence.quote: In a time of war, AI, greed and bad workmanship this company and their work is such a breath of fresh air.

evidence.claim: Viewers single out one new engineering idea as remarkable.
evidence.quote: The spiral neck skeleton is genius.

evidence.claim: Viewers respond to the enthusiasm the host and expert share.
evidence.quote: Their shared enthusiasm for art is so contagious.

evidence.claim: The armature's realistic anatomy makes it appealing beyond animation fans.
evidence.quote: this armature can almost be used to teach bird skeletal anatomy

card.time_to_reproduce: Puppet: months to years for a studio team, since the creator says it 'took years of development'. A similar BTS walkthrough video: 1-3 days of shooting and editing if you have access to a puppet.

card.title: Tiny Clay Baby vs Dangerous Lion 🦁😱 | Emotional Clay Animation Story | Miniature Village
card.sub_style: claimed claymation miniature-village narrative short (story + miniature cooking payoff); the production method has not been verified
card.summary: A 187-second 'clay animation' story set in a miniature clay village. A tiny baby faces a lion to save his friends, and the story ends with a fish-curry meal. It mixes three popular formats: a cute character in danger, a cosy miniature world, and a miniature-cooking payoff. It got about 523k views in 26 days on a channel with 256 followers (about 2,044 views per follower). Possibly that reach came from browse/suggested traffic rather than subscribers, but this is a guess: the thumbnail was not seen and no traffic-source data was available. Only the title and description were available, so the actual technique could not be checked. It might be physical stop-motion, digital clay-style 3D, or AI-generated.
how_it_is_made: likely: Write a simple three-act story: a hungry baby and his mother, then the lion threatens the children, then a brave rescue and a happy ending with a shared meal (all from the description).
likely: Sculpt the characters (baby, mother, children, lion) in polymer or oil-based clay over wire armatures so they can be posed.
likely: Build a tabletop miniature village set (huts, ground, props, tiny cooking pots) at the same scale as the characters.
likely: Shoot frame by frame on a locked-off camera with continuous lighting, at about 12 fps on twos so the clay look reads clearly.
likely: Film the fish-curry cooking finale as close-up miniature-food shots, the payoff that cooking audiences expect.
likely: Add music, sound effects and possibly emotional sting cues in editing, then export landscape for YouTube along with a high-contrast lion-vs-baby thumbnail.

Alternative (unverified): the whole piece could be AI-generated video in a clay style, a common approach for small channels putting out long 'clay village' stories. Check this against the frames before reproducing.

card.title: Claude Opus 5.5 Animated Every Motion Graphic in This Video (I Didn't Keyframe a Thing)
card.sub_style: AI-prompted React/Remotion motion graphics overlays (graphic types unverified; a commenter mentions a 25-second promo) rendered and composited in CapCut
card.summary: A 15-minute tutorial by Matt Loui in which, he says, every motion graphic was generated by Claude Code writing Remotion (React) compositions. He then rendered them and edited them in CapCut, and says he never keyframed anything by hand. The method rests on three prompting modes: record it, screenshot it, or reference it. Comments also mention two supporting habits: asking Claude to ask clarifying questions, and keeping one chat per video so the style stays consistent. It matters as a reproducible workflow that lets solo editors without After Effects keyframing skills make motion graphics.
how_it_is_made: likely: Set up a Remotion project (React-based programmatic video) and open Claude Code in that project directory.

Choose one of the three prompting modes for each graphic: record it, screenshot it, or reference it. likely: record = a screen recording of the motion you want; screenshot = a still of the target look; reference = an existing example.
likely: Add an instruction such as 'ask me as many questions as you need' so Claude clarifies timing, colours, text and duration before writing code.
Let Claude Code write the Remotion motion graphics. likely: preview in Remotion Studio and iterate by describing changes in plain language instead of adjusting keyframes.
Keep all motion graphics for the same video in one Claude Code chat so the style carries over between graphics.
likely: Render each composition from Remotion to a video file (possibly with alpha, e.g. ProRes 4444/WebM, for overlays).
Import the renders into CapCut.
likely: Place the renders on the CapCut timeline over or between A-roll footage.
likely: Fine-tune placement, cut points and audio sync in CapCut rather than in code.
